comments.author: throw0101a
comments.why: US military video on the theory of celestial navigation
comments.text: > Curious how navigation at night was not possible without expensive equipment, sounds like they were relying only on starts in the morning and evening? As a sibling comment notes, it is possible. There are tables for lunar distance: * [LINK] * [LINK] * [LINK] The planets Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn can be used, as well as several dozen planets (lookup tables in an almanac) * [LINK] * [LINK] Two US military videos explaining the theory (ground points/GP, circle of position, etc ): * USAF: [VIDEO] * Army: [LINK] The USAF has a video because that's how planes used to do navigation outside of radio range—sextants on the ceiling of the cockpit: * [LINK] * [LINK]

comments.author: throw0101b
comments.why: Geocentric celestial sphere makes sextant navigation mathematically easy
comments.text: > I'd think that the Earth rotating would be obvious much, much sooner […] How exactly could you tell the difference between one moving reference and another? Einstein eventually showed us that it is not possible. As this US Navy video shows, having the Earth stand still and having the 'celestial sphere' move actually makes celestial navigation using a sextant possible / mathematically easy: * [VIDEO] / [LINK] The Ancients / pre-Moderns concluded that the stars were on one celestial sphere and the wanderers ( planetes in Greek) were on others.
